title: One visit. Two different stories.
intro: Two fictional opinion pieces share an event and its facts. They differ in emphasis and persuasion. We assess observable features of the writing; readers form their own political opinions.

welcomes_visit: The author personally welcomes the reception and meeting as a political achievement. Merely accepting the need for talks is not enough.
rights_and_oversight: The author advocates civil rights and independent scrutiny as necessary constraints on politicians. Merely mentioning parliament is not enough.
people_vs_elites: The author pits authentic ordinary people against allegedly detached or self-serving elites. A quoted slogan the author rejects does not count.
leader_over_scrutiny: The author wants greater freedom for a decisive leader and frames scrutiny or critics as obstacles. Praise for negotiation alone is not enough.
authorial_persuasion: The author repeatedly evaluates, recommends or uses irony. This can apply to either viewpoint. It does not measure truthfulness.
evaluative_labels: The author repeatedly uses praise/blame labels in their own voice.
discrediting_opponents: The author dismisses a position by disparaging its supporters.
us_vs_them: The author endorses a moral division between groups.

threshold_note: The default thresholds for present / absent are 85% support for that option and 60% confidence. The actual thresholds are shown for each question. Otherwise the result is Review. These are experimental thresholds. Confidence is not measured accuracy; the probabilities describe the model's answer distribution. The preview does not invent measurements.
limits: A present feature is not praise, and an absent feature is not a defect. Both supplied texts are opinion pieces. Features can coexist; they are not universal definitions of liberalism or populism. Results do not establish hidden intent, coordination, factual truth or the author's political identity. Queue routing is an illustrative application rule.
reference_title: Author's reference key — open after making your own assessment
reference_note: Writing intent: A uses a liberal-institutional frame, B a populist frame. Both present an intelligible argument. These are manually prepared expectations and excerpts, not Jev results or explanations. The key is never sent to the model. An excerpt illustrates authorial intent; absence of a feature in particular must be judged from the whole article.
identical: Control pair: both inputs are identical. Different model results would call for a stability check, not establish a difference between the texts.

translation_title: A side observation: translation as another framing layer
translation_context: This example was created to explain the integration and compare writing styles. Independently assessing its English and Czech texts suggested another possible use: comparing an original with a free translation for shifts in emphasis, evaluation or whose opinion is being expressed.
translation_limits: A difference can point to passages worth checking. It does not by itself show that a translation changed the framing: language sensitivity and variation between model runs can also affect the scores. This is a follow-up idea from the teaching experiment, not a validated translation check.

methodology.title: How we designed this assessment
methodology.intro: The model answers the questions we chose. A result describes those criteria in this text; it is not a universal score of the writer’s bias.
steps: The original visit preset separates endorsement of the visit, advocacy of oversight, people-versus-elites rhetoric, freedom for a leader and authorial persuasion. For another purpose, choose other observable features separately.
Define present, absent and unclear for each feature. Specify that a quoted view is not automatically the author’s own position. Each complete article is sent separately with the same questions.
Jev returns an answer distribution and confidence. The application applies the configured probability and confidence thresholds; unclear or insufficient support leads to review.
The application then uses a chosen feature for routing, or simply compares the feature profiles. No political opinion earns an overall quality grade.
methodology.scope: Welcoming this visit is specific to the event. Rights/oversight, people versus elites and leader versus scrutiny describe political frames, not bias by themselves. Authorial persuasion is more broadly usable. For a product review, scientific article or another political event, choose and validate the features relevant to that task. These questions cannot reveal omitted facts without additional sources or establish a writer’s hidden motives.

methodology.adapt_title: How to adapt this to your own text
adapt: Start with the decision you need. Replace “Is this biased?” with a feature you can point to: repeated authorial praise/blame, disparagement of opponents, or an endorsed us-versus-them contrast.
Define both a positive example and a near miss. An author endorsing a claim differs from reporting it or quoting it critically. A strong opinion alone does not establish factual error.
Remove event-specific assumptions. If you want stance toward a particular actor or proposal, name that target in the question; the generic feature profile does not identify it automatically.
Keep the same questions for comparable texts. Include neutral reporting, commentary, irony and attributed quotations in your test set. Hand-label cases before looking at model output.
Version wording and thresholds, keep a separate evaluation set, and inspect uncertain as well as confident answers. The rhetoric preset is a starting point, not a validated universal method.
